newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Yeltsin vows to launch new anti-corruption drive.
newsitem.headline: Yeltsin vows to launch new anti-corruption drive.

text.p: President Boris Yeltsin declared war on corruption on Thursday and said he was determined to defeat the age-old demon of Russian political life once and for all.
"I know that you will nevertheless have your doubts about our victory over corruption," the president said in a regular radio address.
"But I am determined, I have the political will and I have your backing in this fight. I will bring this difficult struggle to an end. It will become scary to steal and to take bribes."

Yeltsin has launched several anti-corruption drives but bribery and corruption have flourished at all levels of government since the end of communist rule in 1991. There has been little evidence of success and few criminal convictions.
Yeltsin said his new effort would open up the system of tendering for state orders to reduce the temptation faced by bureaucrats, and he vowed to increase the state's authority.

"Corruption is one of the main reasons that the authority of the Russian state is low today. This is preventing us from bringing order to the country and threatening the very security of Russia," he said.
The 66-year-old president's harsh words were part of efforts to show Russians he is trying to bring order to political life and the economy after a long absence with ill health.
He has also criticised his government, reshuffled the cabinet and brought in young liberal reformers to set economic reforms rolling again.
Also on Thursday the government discussed privatisation plans which have opened the path to capitalism but also created opportunities for bureaucratic self-enrichment on a grand scale.

First Deputy Prime Minister Anatoly Chubais, the father of Russia's privatisation programme, chaired the meeting in the absence of Prime Minister Viktor Chernomyrdin, who is on a two-day holiday to celebrate his 59th birthday.
Chubais said the government needed to focus on earning money from privatising its assets in the next stage of the massive process, RIA news agency reported.
The government should also keep its shares in companies that can be run efficiently, he said. The report said the Russian government holds shares in 2,900 enterprises.

Deputy Prime Minister Alfred Kokh later told reporters the Russian government expected this year to earn 10 trillion roubles ($1.7 billion), up from earlier targets of 6.5 trillion roubles ($1.1 billion), in privatisation revenue.
Although privatisation lies at the core of his economic policy, Yeltsin said last month that bureaucratic red tape and graft had caused stagnation and turned people against reforms.
First Deputy Prime Minister Boris Nemtsov is due to chair a meeting on Saturday to pin down details of how to ensure federal contracts are filled by fair and open tender.

"This theme will find full support in the State Duma," the lower house of parliament's chairman, Gennady Seleznyov, was quoted by Interfax news agency as saying on Yeltsin's anti-corruption initiative.
Sweetheart deals with federal contractors are seen as a major source of illicit income for some officials.
Yeltsin also seems keen to show a firm hand, both to the government and to his opponents in parliament, before leaving for a holiday after an official visit to Germany next week.
Yeltsin will then host Chinese President Jiang Zemin from April 22 to 26 in the latest sign of improving relations.
